memory_leads.lead: The master/bridge team remains the onboard navigation decision layer while shore operations and commercial weather-routing advisers can supply forecasts, route alternatives and performance guidance; advice and navigational responsibility should remain distinct states rather than one automated route choice.

Forecast information and observed onboard conditions are separate information states. A voyage plan may be rational under the latest forecast yet require revision when later forecasts or actual wind, waves, visibility or pressure systems diverge.
Weather-routing is a repeated voyage-control loop—forecast, compare route/speed options, execute, observe, reforecast and revise—rather than a single pre-sailing path selection.

Wind direction and strength affect speed made good, propulsion load, fuel use and maneuvering exposure differently depending on heading and vessel characteristics; the structural category is relative wind effect rather than an exact performance coefficient.

Wave and swell height, period and direction create a sea-state constraint distinct from wind alone. Ship motion, slamming, green water, propeller emergence or voluntary speed reduction can lower realized speed even when engine power is available.

Ocean currents can be favorable or adverse and can alter speed over ground and route economics without changing through-water propulsion demand; routing therefore depends on both atmosphere and ocean state.

Heavy-weather avoidance can trade additional distance against reduced exposure and higher achievable safe speed. The shortest geographic route is therefore not always the fastest, safest or lowest-fuel realized voyage.

Tropical-cyclone or severe-storm avoidance creates dynamic exclusion and timing decisions around forecast track, uncertainty and vessel position; exact storms, safety thresholds and route decisions are deferred to Evidence.

Weather-induced speed loss is an independent effective-capacity mechanism: repeated slower voyages increase round-trip duration and absorb vessel days even when the fleet, route distance and scheduled frequency are unchanged.

Cargo condition and securing risk can be weather-sensitive. Ship motion and water exposure can raise damage risk or trigger operational precautions, linking voyage hydrometeorology to the P013/P014 evidence and cargo-handling chains without establishing any specific casualty.

Ice navigation introduces an additional route-access state involving ice presence/forecast, vessel capability, speed restrictions or route avoidance and, in some contexts, organized assistance; exact ice-class, seasonal and authority rules are deferred.
Fog, poor visibility and precipitation can change bridge workload, safe speed and collision-avoidance margin on open-water or coastal legs even outside the harbor/VTS stoppage state captured in P022.

Weather-route decisions interact with commercial ETA commitments: a master or operator may accept extra distance, delay or reduced speed to preserve safety margins, while downstream terminals, charter administration or liner connections react to the revised ETA.
The atlas effective-versus-nominal-capacity theme should include stochastic voyage-duration loss from weather and current, not only congestion, rerouting, speed policy and regulation.

The atlas fuel-speed tradeoff is refined because voluntary slow steaming, weather-imposed speed loss and storm-avoidance deviation are economically different causes of lower realized speed and fuel consumption; replay should not collapse them.

P019 schedule reliability depends on forecast-vintage and route-revision timing: weather risk known before departure, discovered en route and actually experienced should remain separate when reconstructing why an ETA changed.

Schedule recovery after adverse weather can increase later speed/fuel use or compress port buffers, so one weather delay can propagate into downstream operating choices rather than remaining an isolated voyage-time loss.
The broad claim that weather can disrupt shipping and chokepoints is already present in the atlas; P024 retains only voyage-scale forecast/routing and performance mechanics.
Local weather/visibility interruptions to pilotage, tug and port movements were already captured by P022; P024 is limited to voyage-scale hydrometeorology outside that port-call readiness layer.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind memory supports the advisory/decision role but cannot establish historical product capabilities, model versions, provider rankings or algorithmic performance.
Exact storm tracks, route choices, delay durations and ice seasons require dated source-first Evidence.
Performance depends on hull, loading, machinery, sea state and measurement method; exact numerical relationships require vessel- and source-specific Evidence.
Current conditions are explicitly outside blind historical-memory scope and require live source-first information.

stop_reason: The voyage-scale hydrometeorology chain is populated from forecast/observation and advisory roles through route/speed revision, wind/wave/current/storm/ice effects and downstream ETA/fuel/cargo/capacity consequences. Further recall becomes storm-, route-, provider-, forecast-product-, vessel-performance- or current-condition-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no forecast accuracy, provider capability, storm/ice event, route deviation, weather delay, vessel performance coefficient, casualty or current condition is verified.
